articles.title: Líderes discursam na sessão de alto nível da COP31; acompanhe ao vivo
articles.summary: Lula foi anunciado no momento previsto para seu discurso, mas não falou. Mais cedo, discursou na abertura da Cúpula dos Líderes e, rouco, pediu ao ministro do Meio Ambiente que lesse outra fala.
articles.body:
Lula foi anunciado no momento previsto para seu discurso, mas não falou. Mais cedo, discursou na abertura da Cúpula dos Líderes e, rouco, pediu ao ministro do Meio Ambiente que lesse outra fala.

A sessão de alto nível da COP31, com pronunciamentos de chefes de Estado e de governo, foi encerrada nesta quarta-feira (11). Lula chegou a ser anunciado, mas não discursou. Mais cedo, o presidente brasileiro havia falado na abertura da Cúpula de Líderes.

O presidente de Palau, Surangel Whipps Jr., discursa agora na sessão de alto nível da COP31.

Lula, que estava previsto para falar antes dele, chegou a ser anunciado, mas não discursou. Ainda não há confirmação de quando o presidente brasileiro poderá fazer seu pronunciamento.

Pela ordem provisória da ONU, o pronunciamento nacional de Lula deveria ocorrer neste momento na sessão de alto nível da COP31. O presidente chegou a ser anunciado, mas não discursou.

Mais cedo, Lula falou na abertura da Cúpula de Líderes e, devido à rouquidão, pediu que o ministro do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, João Paulo Capobianco, lesse outro discurso durante um encontro sobre florestas.

Agora discursa Alexander Van der Bellen, presidente da Áustria. Pela lista provisória da ONU, Lula é o próximo a falar na plenária da COP31, caso a sequência seja mantida.

O presidente das Maldivas, Mohamed Muizzu, discursa neste momento na COP31. Segundo a lista provisória da ONU, o próximo a falar é o presidente da Áustria, Alexander Van der Bellen, seguido pelo presidente brasileiro, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. A ordem dos pronunciamentos pode sofrer alterações.

Agora discursa Denis Sassou Nguesso, presidente da República do Congo.

Agora discursa Alexander Stubb, presidente da Finlândia.

O presidente do Sudão, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, discursa neste momento na sessão de alto nível da COP31, em Antália, na Turquia. Lula também está na lista de líderes que devem fazer pronunciamentos nacionais nesta quarta-feira (11).

'Cada fração de grau importa', alerta presidente da Comissão Europeia

Ursula von der Leyen chamou o último verão europeu de “ verão da verdade ”, ao lembrar do calor extremo e da alta dos preços da energia.

Ela alertou que o mundo caminha para ultrapassar o limite de aquecimento de 1,5°C.

A dirigente também afirmou que a União Europeia deve reduzir suas emissões em mais da metade até 2030. Mas projeções oficiais apontam um corte de 54%, abaixo da meta de 55%.

A presidente da Comissão Europeia, Ursula von der Leyen, discursa neste momento na plenária da COP31, em Antália, na Turquia.

A presidente da Tanzânia, Samia Suluhu Hassan, discursa neste momento na plenária principal da COP31, em Antália. É a quinta chefe de Estado a falar nesta quarta.

Embora cada país tenha três minutos, os discursos têm se estendido, e a fila avança mais devagar que o previsto. O presidente Lula é o 20º da lista e, no ritmo atual, deve discursar no fim da tarde no horário local, início da tarde em Brasília.

Em outro momento do discurso, Lula afirmou que a COP31 terá a missão de “devolver à mudança do clima a atenção que ela merece”. Leia como foi o discurso completo.

Lula afirmou que a crise climática também é uma crise de justiça de classe, gênero e raça, além de refletir desigualdades entre os países. Segundo o presidente, não faz sentido abandonar o princípio das responsabilidades comuns, porém diferenciadas, já que os países ricos se desenvolveram às custas do planeta e precisam cumprir seus compromissos.

O presidente também destacou que a próxima COP, em solo africano, representa uma oportunidade histórica para garantir mais recursos a um continente que, segundo ele, se encontra estrangulado.

"O Brasil vai fazer sua parte. Adotando o mapa do caminho para reduzir a dependência de combustíveis fortes e eliminar o desmatamento e a degradação da floresta", diz.

O presidente afirma ainda que o planeta não pode ficar à mercê de disputa de hegemônicas. "Secas, enchentes, incêndios e elevação do nível do mar já fazem parte da realidade das pessoas".

"No início deste ano, a mudança do clima desapareceu dos discursos e dos documentos das lideranças globais", afirma o presidente. Lula disse ainda que "passamos a falar mais de armas do que sobrevivência da futura gerações".

Bom dia, o presidente do Brasil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, começa o seu discurso na COP31.

articles.title: Joe Biden, in His Only New Interview, Goes on Camera with PEOPLE to Talk About Everything (Exclusive)
articles.summary: Speaking with PEOPLE at his home in Wilmington, Del., the former president opens up about living with stage 4 prostate cancer, revelations in his new memoir...
articles.body:
Joe Biden gets candid about his stage 4 prostate cancer as he releases his new memoir , Promise Me, America

The former president reflects on life, withdrawing from the 2024 race and the legacy he hopes to leave

Dr. Jill Biden describes the daily realities of caring for her husband with support from their family

Two days after the Democrats swept the midterm elections , former President Joe Biden has that signature twinkle in his blue eyes.

"Look at the people we got elected: first women governors, first Black governors," he tells PEOPLE with a quiet rasp.

At 83, and living with stage 4 prostate cancer — for which he completed radiation and is undergoing hormone therapy — Biden is slower than when he suddenly withdrew from the presidential race in 2024 following a disastrous debate against Donald Trump and amid concerns about his health. Still, his perennial optimism remains.

"I'm not saying I'll live forever," says the one-term president, seated in the dining room of his Wilmington, Del., lake house, "but the point is that I have all my faculties, I have access to all the things I had before and I feel good."

He's fighting the disease "like hell," Biden writes in his presidential memoir, Promise Me, America , out Nov. 17. Through it all, his wife, Dr. Jill Biden , 75, has been by his side. Being a family caregiver — like 63 million Americans — is "emotionally, physically hard," the former first lady says after returning home from volunteering at a women's prison, where she teaches literature part-time.

Although she has help looking after her husband and says family is a constant at the house, "My days are making sure he eats right. Does he exercise? Is he taking the right medicine? Did I talk to the doctor?"

Reality came into focus when she read a magazine at a nail salon and imagined traveling to the destinations on the glossy pages. "All of a sudden it struck me, like, 'Wait a minute, this isn't our life now,' " she says. "We're on a new journey."

With no questions off the table, President Biden addresses his life and health now, his presidency and the legacy he hopes to leave behind.

In May 2025, 118 days after you left office, you announced that you had been diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer that had spread to your bones. You write that you're fighting it with the "help of an incredible medical team and an even better family." What does that fight look like?

It looks very positive. There's a lot of people who've been diagnosed with cancer, particularly the kind of cancer I have, who live long lives, who live for another 10, 20 years. And so far, the two tests that have been done show that the cancer is not metastasized beyond what it already was ... There are eight different pills I take a day.

Next June will mark your 50th wedding anniversary. What has cancer taught you about your marriage that you didn't know before?

Nothing. I knew from the beginning what she was. Jill is, first of all, bright as hell. Secondly, I think she's the most beautiful woman in the world, which every husband probably thinks, but I believe it. And we have a real partnership.

How has your family, including your grandchildren and your great-grandchild, supported you?

They're always here. "Can we come up, Pop? Pop, can we do this?" I do more with my grandchildren than I do with anybody else, and that's for real. I'm interested and they're interested in serious things as well ... They're involved in a lot of things having to do with public service. They participate in a number of issues that relate to the well-being of the country. They're the loves of my life.

As the second Catholic to become president, you've been candid about how your faith has guided you through hard times. Do you still see signs of those you've lost?

I do. I see signs of their love in their progeny. I see signs of their love of things that I find out that they have done that I didn't know they had done before ... My son Hunter , he and his brother Beau were born a year and a day apart. They're each other's best friends in the world. When Beau died, it was a blow to Hunter in a way that was almost beyond repair ... Now he's deeply involved in public policy things. He's deeply involved in making the case, but he's straight as an arrow in terms of his alcoholism. My dad used to have an expression: "Joey, family's the beginning, the middle and the end." And that's how it is.

You write, "People say I was deluding myself that I could do the job [of president] at my age. My answer to that is: I was doing the job." Why do you think they felt that way?

It's natural. If tomorrow you're going to say that the head of your [company] is going to be hired on as an 80-year-old person, you go, "What the hell's going on?" But the value I think I brought was I knew so many of the leaders, I knew their inclinations, I knew what was going on, and many of them came to me. I thought it was value added, not subtracted.

Standard medical guidelines don't recommend routine prostate cancer screenings for men over 70. You write, "I was treated no differently from any other 82-year-old man in America. Maybe I should have been." What do you say to Americans who believe that a screening should have been part of your annual physical?

Look, White House doctors are doing what the whole entire medical profession is doing ... I had some discomfort, and Jill thought, Why isn't that test done for men who are in their 70s? And there wasn't any particular [sign] except recurring pain.

You describe a "cynical twist" on your cancer news: that some folks said you hid your cancer as president. Why do you think they reacted that way?

A lot of people do that. They hide bad news from the public if they're elected officials. I didn't do that. We let the public know when I found out, when I knew what was going on. I think it's important for a national leader, as president, to let people know they go through some of the very same things that a lot of American people are going through ... I wasn't hiding it at all.

Many have spoken about the toll of the Presidency. How might your undiagnosed cancer have exacerbated that?

First of all, I never felt the toll. I read [others] like Harry Truman talk about [how] it's the most difficult job in the world. I didn't find it that way. And so I, quite frankly, found that it didn't in any way interfere with my job.

What do you miss the most about the job?

The staff, the people in the White House. They're good people, from the people making sure there's a sheet on the bed to the people who are taking care of all the visitors that come through. They all have a sense of honor, what they're doing in the White House. It's the People's House.

What's your reaction to the Trump ballroom and the East Wing being destroyed?

Almost as disturbing as the gold bars on the walls of the White House and the Oval Office. I mean, what the hell are we talking about? I find it disturbing ... I've viewed the president's judgment in tearing down the East Wing and a number of other things as nothing more than to try to create monuments to himself: "I built that." I find it beneath the country.

It's been two years and four months since that debate moment on the stage with Trump. What is your perspective on it now?

Look, I don't know anybody who hasn't made a mistake in a debate. To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there'd be another debate, which there wasn't. But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn't another debate, it didn't disturb me because it wasn't consequential.

In hindsight, looking at the 2024 election, is there anything you would've done differently?

What I can't say, because there's no evidence of it — if I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have resigned. I would've not gone forward, because I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for [president]. But that wasn't the case ... I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job.

Hunter has been speaking out on podcasts and social media. What do you make of that?

Hunter is one of the brightest men I know. He has more moral and physical courage than most people I know, and I'm really proud of him. He's making the case as to how we should proceed as a country.

He's said of the pardon you gave him: "Was it good for our Constitution? Was it good for the American people? Was it good for my father's legacy? No on all accounts." What's your perspective?

I disagree ... I watched the modus operandi of Trump. He goes after people without any basis, whether they're viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do. If I hadn't pardoned — not just some of my family members, anyone who's dealt with me—he would go back and try to do harm to them, as I've observed.

In your book, for the first time, you share the letter that Trump left you in the Oval Office after you beat him in the 2020 election. Your takeaway: "It was almost as if there were two Donald Trumps." What do you mean?

That could have been written by President Kennedy to me or by President Johnson or by George Bush. I mean, it was gracious, it was generous, and it was totally inconsistent with the kind of president he'd been.

You write, "Promise me, America, that we will be the nation we know in our hearts we can be and should be." What does that nation mean to you at 83, after more than 50 years of public service?

It means to continue to hold those truths to be self-evident, that we're all created equal. I got involved in politics because of the Civil Rights movement. It means to be engaged in trying to help make the country a better place than it has been, to give people the benefit of the doubt ... When I say, "Promise me, America," I mean, America, you know the promises we made. Let's keep them.

How do you want the American people to remember you?

I tell you, it's the greatest honor any man or woman could be given anywhere to be the President of the United States of America. And I hope I kept the promise of America ... I didn't say I didn't make mistakes—but I meant what I said, and I did what I said I was going to do.

articles.title: White House confronts Democrats over planned probes, claiming possible 'criminality'
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that su...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress -- may amount to "blatant criminality."

White House counsel Will Scharf issued the warning in a letter dated Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

Garcia most likely would chair the powerful panel in the new Democratic-controlled Congress that is seated in January. Garcia warned Trump officials to "lawyer up" as his party was on the way to stunning victories in last week's midterm election.

In response, Scharf wrote that "threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality." The letter's existence was first reported by Punchbowl News.

Garcia said in response to the letter that "it appears Donald Trump has something to hide" and stressed that Congress' investigative powers do not need the "permission of the White House."

"Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate," Garcia said. "The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse."

Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.

Garcia also wants to look at the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations . Other targets include Trump's White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family's role in mineral deals and Trump's crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a CNN interview that aired Sunday that "there could be" a crime to investigate if rhetoric from Democrats turned threatening. He appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone during an appearance in Missouri this week, saying "Congress has oversight authority. It always has, it always will. The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it's through subpoenas or letters — so we're not going to stop working with Congress."

"Nothing I've said this weekend, or in the past, should suggest otherwise," he added.

Some lawmakers cautioned Democrats as well as the White House against overreaching.

Outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Trump critic, said he hopes Democrats don't squander their new powers on "stupid things."

"I hope they have real hearings about real things, not another Russiagate," he said, referring to a previous congressional inquiry into ties between Trump's first presidential campaign in 2016 and Russia. Trump repeatedly denounced that investigation as a "hoax."

"I think there is some real corruption there around the fringes," Massie said about Trump and some of those around the president. Massie lost his primary election to a Trump-backed GOP challenger.

Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., who is expected to be the next House Ethics Committee chairman, said he would not back down from any investigations because of warnings from the White House.

"If they're trying to intimidate, at least for me, it's not going to get me," said DeSaulnier, who was a Republican before he switched to the Democratic Party in 2000. "I don't work for a mafia, a mob organization."

Associated Press writer Eric Tucker and AP video journalist Nathan Ellgren contributed to this report.

articles.title: Surrealista: pierde un partido por golpearse la zapatilla con la pala
articles.standfirst: Nuria Rodríguez y Giulia Dal Pozzo cayeron ante Claudia Jensen y Tamara Icardo, pero el desenlace del encuentro quedó marcado por la decisión arbitral tras un gesto de la primera
articles.summary: Nuria Rodríguez y Giulia Dal Pozzo cayeron ante Claudia Jensen y Tamara Icardo, pero el desenlace del encuentro quedó marcado por la decisión arbitral tras un gesto de la primera
articles.body: La jornada de este miércoles en el Dubái P1 dejó una de las escenas más llamativas de la temporada en Premier Padel. Nuria Rodríguez y Giulia Dal Pozzo se despidieron del torneo en los dieciseisavos de final tras perder por 6-2 y 6-3 frente a Claudia Jensen y Tamara Icardo. Sin embargo, más allá del resultado, toda la atención se centró en una acción que terminó por decidir el encuentro de una manera inesperada. Con Jensen e Icardo a un punto de cerrar el partido, Rodríguez protagonizó un gesto de frustración al golpearse la zapatilla con la pala. La jugadora española ya había recibido una advertencia anteriormente y el árbitro interpretó que aquella acción merecía un segundo warning. Al acumular dos avisos, la sanción implicaba la pérdida automática del punto y, por tanto, el final del encuentro. La resolución sorprendió a las cuatro jugadoras, especialmente por el momento en el que se produjo. Rodríguez mostró inmediatamente su desacuerdo y comenzó a reclamar explicaciones al colegiado. Incluso Claudia Jensen, desde el lado contrario de la pista, pareció no entender la decisión y salió en defensa de la española con una frase contundente: "No es warning". La reacción de la gaditana reflejó la impotencia que sintió al ver cómo el partido terminaba de aquella forma. Con las manos en la cabeza y visiblemente afectada, la española no ocultó su frustración y volvió a hacer referencia a los problemas que, según ella, viene arrastrando con el arbitraje. "Siempre me pasa a mí, te juro que me quiero esconder. Siempre me pasa a mí", expresó Rodríguez, incapaz de encontrar una explicación a lo sucedido. La jugadora continuó mostrando su incredulidad por una sanción que consideraba desproporcionada. "Una pena. No sé cómo lo hago", comentó mientras trataba de asimilar que el desenlace del partido hubiera llegado por una decisión disciplinaria. También cuestionó directamente la interpretación del árbitro y el motivo por el que su gesto había sido considerado merecedor de una segunda advertencia. "Escúchame, ¿cómo puede ser? No puede ser por hacer así. ¿Estamos diciendo algo fuera de lo normal?", protestó durante la discusión. El principal argumento de Rodríguez giraba en torno a la necesidad de mantener una interpretación uniforme de las normas durante los encuentros. "Tienes que tener un criterio. Es que se equivoca todo el rato", insistió, dejando patente su malestar con la actuación arbitral. Lo ocurrido en Dubái no es un caso aislado en la temporada de Nuria Rodríguez. La jugadora ya había protagonizado otro enfrentamiento con el arbitraje durante el London P1 del pasado agosto, cuando competía junto a Giulia Dal Pozzo frente a Marta Ortega y Sofía Araújo. En aquel encuentro se produjo una situación controvertida con una pelota que inicialmente había sido señalada como mala. Tras recurrir a la revisión de vídeo, la acción terminó considerándose buena, aunque la árbitra decidió repetir el punto en lugar de concedérselo a Rodríguez y Dal Pozzo. La resolución provocó una larga discusión sobre la pista y fue necesaria la intervención del supervisor para intentar reconducir la situación. La tensión fue tal que la española llegó a plantearse abandonar la competición si se repetían episodios de ese tipo. Finalmente, fueron Marta Ortega y Sofía Araújo quienes optaron por conceder voluntariamente el punto a sus adversarias

articles.title: Just 40 percent in new poll looking forward to 2028 presidential election
articles.summary: Less than half of Americans are looking forward to the upcoming presidential election, according to a new poll. In the CNN poll, 40 percent of respondents said they are “looking forward to” the 2028 presidential contest, while 27 percent said they are “dreading” the election and 33 percent said they are “neither” looking forward to…
articles.body:
Less than half of Americans are looking forward to the upcoming presidential election , according to a new poll.

In the CNN poll , 40 percent of respondents said they are “looking forward to” the 2028 presidential contest, while 27 percent said they are “dreading” the election and 33 percent said they are “neither” looking forward to nor dreading the next race for the White House.

This year’s midterm elections, in which Democrats scored major victories two years after key losses, are wrapping up. Democrats locked down the House and Senate amid a rocky political environment for the GOP that included issues like the unpopular Iran war, President Trump’s slumping approval numbers and concerns about the cost of living.

The last presidential election was highly chaotic, with attempted assassinations against Trump, a rough debate performance from former President Biden that sparked questions about his health and former Vice President Kamala Harris taking over the Democratic ticket only a few months before Election Day.

When respondents to the CNN poll were asked if they had a “specific person” they would “like to see run for president in 2028,” 35 percent responded in the affirmative and 64 percent responded in the negative.

The next presidential election will also be the first without Trump as a candidate in more than a decade, with the 22nd Amendment barring a president from serving more than two terms .

The CNN poll took place Oct. 15-18 among 1,701 respondents and had a margin of sampling error of 2.9 percentage points.

articles.title: Jim Justice says GOP can ‘forget’ retaking Senate majority in 2028
articles.summary: Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) says his party can “forget” about retaking the Senate majority in 2028 just a week after brutal losses for Republicans on deep-red turf. “You can forget 2028. Absolutely,” Justice told the Washington Examiner. “This is such a colossal blow that it is beyond belief how colossal this is to America.” Democrats…
articles.body:
Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) says his party can “forget” about retaking the Senate majority in 2028 just a week after brutal losses for Republicans on deep-red turf.

“You can forget 2028. Absolutely,” Justice told the Washington Examiner . “This is such a colossal blow that it is beyond belief how colossal this is to America.”

Democrats flipped seven seats in the upper chamber, with two more races — Alaska and Mississippi — outstanding.

The party picked up Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina, Iowa and Kansas and are leading in Alaska and Mississippi — a possible nine-seat gain that would put Democrats at 56 Senate seats, the most a party has won in an election since 2008.

The big gain may make it easier to govern, but it also dramatically increases the likelihood of a Democratic Senate majority beyond 2028.

Even if Democrats lose Alaska and Mississippi, Republicans would need to flip five seats to win back the Senate in 2028, or four if they hold the presidency. The clearest opportunities to do so are Georgia, where Sen. Raphael Warnock (D) is up for reelection, Arizona, where Sen. Mark Kelly (D) is up, Pennsylvania with Sen. John Fetterman’s (D) seat and Nevada with Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto.

So if they win the presidency, those four could be enough. If they lose the presidency, it is not immediately clear where Republicans could have a chance to pick up enough seats, and if they lose the outstanding races in Alaska and Mississippi, their odds look even tougher.

Democrats, meanwhile, may even have a path to the coveted 60 seats in the Senate, a filibuster-proof majority, a feat not achieved since 2010.

The clearest targets for them include Wisconsin with Sen. Ron Johnson (R) and North Carolina with Sen. Ted Budd (R). But Democrats pulled off major victories in places like Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina this year, all three of which have seats up in 2028.

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) ran the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) this cycle, the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm, and announced she would volunteer to head the organization again.

Gillibrand told Nexstar this week that she is already looking to expand her party’s Senate majority in 2028.

“I think there’s more states we can put in play,” Gillibrand said. “There’s a lot of opportunity next cycle that we can try to build on what we did this cycle.”

articles.title: Alina Habba Mildon loses $50M contract after Trump criticism
articles.summary: Alina Habba Mildon, a former attorney for President Trump, has reportedly been fired from a multimillion-dollar contract with a family company tied to a billionaire banker who recently received a presidential pardon. Concord Partners, a Florida-based company established by the daughter of Venezuelan billionaire Julio Herrera Velutini, terminated Mildon’s $50 million contract in a Nov.…
articles.body:
Alina Habba Mildon, a former attorney for President Trump, has reportedly been fired from a multimillion-dollar contract with a family company tied to a billionaire banker who recently received a presidential pardon.

Concord Partners, a Florida-based company established by the daughter of Venezuelan billionaire Julio Herrera Velutini, terminated Mildon’s $50 million contract in a Nov. 4 letter obtained by The New York Times , citing a “failure to perform duties.” A source close to the family said the former Trump attorney’s priorities appeared to have shifted away from the company after Mildon, 42, began dating her now-husband Turhan Mildon, a 25-year-old Turkish investor, earlier this year, according to The New York Times.

Her firing came days after Trump publicly condemned the arrangement, calling it “ totally obnoxious and outrageous ,” and urging the Herrera family to stop paying his former lawyer.

“I thought it was terrible. I told her,” Trump told reporters. “I said I don’t want her paid. I thought we had somebody speak to the people that did it, and she used her relationship to do that.”

Mildon was hired as Concord’s general counsel under a four-year agreement that guaranteed her more than $50 million in salary and bonuses.

Despite her termination, she will retain an $8 million signing bonus and $6.5 million in payments already received, totaling $14.5 million, The New York Times reported.

A person close to Mildon told the outlet she intends to pursue legal action.

Herrera Velutini had faced felony bribery charges stemming from an alleged scheme to influence the governor of Puerto Rico before reaching a plea agreement in August 2025 that reduced the case to a misdemeanor campaign finance violation.

Still seeking to clear his record, Herrera Velutini enlisted Christopher Kise, a former Trump attorney, to help secure a presidential pardon. His daughter, Isabela Herrera, also donated $3.5 million to a Trump-aligned super PAC.

In October 2025, Isabela Herrera established Concord Partners in Florida. Mildon finalized her employment agreement days later, while she was still serving as U.S. attorney in New Jersey, and formally began working for the company on Jan. 1, where she was guaranteed more than $50 million over four years.

Weeks later, Trump granted Herrera Velutini a full and unconditional pardon. Two other defendants in the Puerto Rico bribery case, including former Puerto Rican Gov. Wanda Vázquez Garced, were pardoned at the same time.

Mildon, who was serving as a senior adviser to the attorney general and a special government employee when she began working for Concord, has denied involvement in securing the pardon.

“Any insulation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the D.O.J. [Department of Justice] — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false,” she wrote in a statement posted to social media last month.

articles.body:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) on Tuesday backed up Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“So, of course, I’m supportive of impeaching Secretary Hegseth. I think that Massie’s articles are completely legitimate. So, I also believe that we’ll see,” Ocasio-Cortez said outside the Capitol on Tuesday night when asked about her vote on impeachment and the future of the effort.

“You know, I think that given how the margins were, it’s possible that Massie would bring this up again, and I think it’s entirely possible that we — it could pass as well,” she added.

On Tuesday, House Republicans shelved a measure spearheaded by Massie that would’ve resulted in a vote on impeaching Hegseth.

The House, via a 211-204 vote, referred the resolution to committee, effectively ending efforts to impeach the defense secretary due to the Iran war and other issues until next year.

Every Democrat in attendance voted for advancing the measure in the Tuesday procedural vote, with Massie being the only Republican to vote across the aisle.

Massie has been a public critic of the U.S. war against Iran, which has also proved to be unpopular with the American public.

The Kentucky Republican had introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth and accused him of abusing U.S. military operations in Yemen, Iran, the Caribbean, the Eastern Pacific and the military operation that captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year.

Democrats are set to take over the House and Senate next year, giving them a better shot at impeaching Hegseth if they do so after Congress changes hands.

articles.title: Data centers losing everywhere, just like crazy far left wants
articles.summary: If you want your county to have money to pay for things, then you have to let your community raise revenue. When you say no to a data center, you are killing your lifeline, maybe the last one you’re going to have.
articles.body:
Well, the results are in, and yes, many Americans do not want data centers built in their neighborhoods. In the midterm elections, there were more than 40 data center moratoriums on the ballot, and all but one of them appear to have passed. I say that’s a shame, but the people have spoken, and so they are going to get exactly what they want. Which is nothing.

Indeed, this is a moral panic being whipped up by anti-growth losers who are doing the bidding of, guess who, the Chinese Communist Party. Mostly unwittingly, because we are not talking about very bright people.

Take, for instance, Taylor Frazier McCollum, a resident of Prince George’s County, Md., who successfully thwarted a $5 billion data center project there. She was recently profiled by NPR , which hailed her as an unexpected activist. The photo in the NPR article shows McCollum posing in front of the land that would have been used: an abandoned, vacant lot that once held a mall that closed down in 2002. Ever since then, this land has been put to no good economic use at all. And now it’s going to stay that way, thanks to McCollum.

Here she was, accepting an award from a pro-environmentalist group, explaining what she did.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is an activist group linked to the pro-China billionaire Roy Singham and the Chinese Communist Party. They are communists and degrowthers and, frankly, enemies of human civilization. McCollum is just their unwitting puppet.

But with their help, she got her way. No more data center. Now the land will continue to be used for nothing. Creating no value for anyone, not the tech sector, and not the community.

And not for McCollum either. According to the NPR profile, she fell on hard times, was evicted from the house she was renting and, along with her young daughter, had to move in with her grandfather, whose house needs a new roof. She even petitioned the county council to create a public fund that would help give people in the community the money they need to fix their roofs, but at the meeting, the council members told her the county is running out of money. A local Six Flags closed, the Washington Commanders, the DC football team, is going to be leaving the county, and so on. The area is in economic decline. But hey, at least, she stopped that data center.

You probably see where I’m going with this. If you want your county to have money to pay for things, then you have to let your community raise revenue. When you say no to a data center, you are killing your lifeline, maybe the last one you’re going to have. Too many communities throughout the country are dying off because they say no to sensible growth and investment. It’s a sad story.

It’s additionally sad that Prince George’s County isn’t a one-off — this is happening all over. Democrats are the anti-data-center party, and they just won huge majorities in national government. At the state level, 75 percent of Americans now have a Democratic governor who is probably going to try to put the brakes on as many of these projects as possible. And the newly ascendant left, in the national Congress, wants to block all new construction everywhere all at once.

I shudder to think what this will mean for economic growth in this country. But at least someone is happy about it: the Chinese Communist Party.

articles.title: Hegseth impeachment blocked despite numerous failings
articles.summary: The writing is on the wall. It’s time for you to go, Pete Hegseth.
articles.body:
Republicans saved Pete Hegseth and voted to block consideration on articles of impeachment against the Defense secretary. It was a temporary move that just kicks the can down the road for Hegseth to face the music at a later date. We haven’t seen Hegseth face reporters at the Pentagon since the summer. But when he was facing impeachment, suddenly he was front and center, taking aim at one of his Republican critics, Congressman Thomas Massie.

But what I witnessed was a sternly delivered political performance that seemed designed for one audience in particular: President Trump.

As MS NOW’s Kyle Griffin pointed out on X: “Pete Hegseth hadn’t addressed reporters at the Pentagon since May. Not even when a Navy commander was killed in a helicopter crash in the Arabian Sea on July 1. Or when three U.S. soldiers were killed in an Iranian missile attack on a base in Jordan on July 17. He waited until he needed to defend himself.”

And Hegseth was making the case for why Trump should keep him around, calling it the “honor of a lifetime” to serve under the president and describing him as the “greatest commander-in-chief.”

Apparently, the performance landed. Trump took to Truth Social to give Hegseth an enthusiastic endorsement . “Pete Hegseth gets an “A” PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie,” Trump said.

Hegseth argued that this impeachment effort also puts troops at risk : “Put the secretary on trial today and the men and women who carried out those orders tomorrow. If they want to come for the warriors they’re going to have to come through me.”

Except this was not an impeachment resolution against American troops. It was an effort to hold the secretary accountable for decisions that may have violated our laws.

Massie explained one of the central arguments on X:

“IMPEACHMENT, Article III The law requires our military to withdraw from hostilities within 60 days if Congress does not authorize the activity. Operation Epic Fury has been underway for 256 days. Congress has not authorized it. Hegseth is breaking the law.”

And here’s Massie’s message for the troops : “This secretary has used our troops to go seize oil for large corporations in America. You shouldn’t be used like that. You signed up to pledge your life for this country if need be, and that obligation shouldn’t be diminished to stealing oil for big corporations.”

Democrats and Republicans alike have questioned the administration’s military actions.

The impeachment resolution raised allegations involving extrajudicial killings, unauthorized military operations, the capture of Venezuela’s former president, Nicolás Maduro, and civilian casualties.

Take the boat strikes targeting suspected drug traffickers. An Associated Press investigation found that the people killed had varying backgrounds, including laborers and struggling locals, and that claims connecting them to drug trafficking were disputed. More than 200 people have reportedly been killed. Families from Trinidad and Tobago are also pursuing legal action against the United States, alleging their relatives were fishermen and farmers, not drug traffickers.

This is why due process matters. An allegation is not a conviction, and suspected criminals are still entitled to their day in court.

Here’s Republican Sen. Rand Paul questioning the legality of the strikes: “The Constitution says that when you go to war, Congress has to vote on it. … The drug war, or the crime war, has typically been dealt with through law enforcement, and so far they have alleged that these people are drug dealers … and we’ve had no evidence presented. So at this point we would call them extrajudicial killings.”

And then there’s the civilian protection issue, which I find particularly troubling. The resolution questions whether Hegseth weakened safeguards designed to prevent civilian deaths, including cuts to the Pentagon’s Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response program and Civilian Protection Center of Excellence. Reported staffing reductions have left these efforts dramatically diminished. These are the very people and resources designed to help prevent tragedies like bombing schools.

Separate from the impeachment allegations are a list of concerns, including misleading the public on ammunition and equipment shortages, forcing out senior military officers during wartime, and blocking merit-based promotions while targeting female leaders and officers of color.

So thanks for that fiery and defensive speech that got you brownie points from the president, but the writing is on the wall. The country spoke in the last election. It’s time for you to go, Pete Hegseth. If you don’t chose to leave on your own terms now, I’m sure you’ll be impeached in January when Democrats take control of both houses of Congress.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Kentucky district election decided by coin flip
articles.summary: This comes as two other Kentucky elections this year were also decided by chance after candidates tied.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — An election in Kentucky ‘s smallest county was reportedly decided by a coin flip last week, marking at least the third time this happened in the state this year.

In the race for magistrate in the 2nd Magisterial District in Robertson County , Republican Benny Ray Renner and Democrat Kristen Gifford Fryman tied with 91 votes each, WLKY reported . The county is located near the Kentucky-Ohio border, less than 60 miles from Cincinnati.

Officials used a coin flip to break the tie after the Kentucky State Board of Elections recommended the method, according to WLKY. Fryman won and will serve on the county’s fiscal court, which sets budget and tax rates, USA Today reported , citing the state of Kentucky.

“When it was tied, I was like, ‘Wow,’” Fryman told WEKU . “I was kind of shocked cause that’s just something I don’t think that…I was told that’s never happened in our county before.”

This comes as two other Kentucky elections this year were also decided by chance after candidates tied. NewsNation local affiliate WEHT reported the Hanson city commissioner race this month and the Union County magistrate race in June came down to the flip of a coin.

articles.title: Kate Middleton says she found ‘hope’ in nature amid cancer journey
articles.summary: Kate Middleton shared in 2024 she was diagnosed with cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Kate Middleton has opened up about the lessons she learned during her cancer fight .

In a rare interview with Country Life magazine, which was edited by Prince William, Kate spoke about recovering from cancer and the difficulties of that period of her life.

“I was told in (a) hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time,” the Princess of Wales said. “This is the same in nature. It shows us that periods of rest, reflection and renewal are equally as important as moments of growth.”

Kate noted that people instinctively turn to the outdoors as a form of healing, adding science now supports that belief.

“Whether it is the beach for healing and recovery, the countryside for peace and perspective or the mountains to find solitude, people have long sought comfort in the natural world,” she told the magazine.

“It is such a restorative environment and incorporating nature into someone’s recovery pathway is vital,” she continued. “Having a sense of connection, trusted people around you and places where you feel at peace can be incredibly important during difficult times.”

The Princess of Wales revealed in March 2024 that she was diagnosed with cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following an absence from the public eye and royal duties.

Kate revealed in January 2025 that her cancer is in remission, writing on social media that she felt a sense of “relief” but remained “focused on recovery.”

articles.title: These 5 House Democrats say traffic caused them to miss Hegseth vote
articles.summary: Eleven Democrats missed a consequential vote in the House Tuesday on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, allowing Republicans to band together and shut down the effort. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) was the only Republican who joined Democrats on the losing side on a 211-204 vote, a seven-vote margin. Most of the members who missed have…
articles.body:
Eleven Democrats missed a consequential vote in the House Tuesday on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, allowing Republicans to band together and shut down the effort.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) was the only Republican who joined Democrats on the losing side on a 211-204 vote, a seven-vote margin.

Most of the members who missed have provided varying explanations for their absence, including at least five who said traffic issues prevented them from voting in time.

Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) released a statement from her office, posting on the social platform X that she arrived right after the voting period ended.

“Like other Members of Congress, Rep. Stansbury was blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote,” her office said.

Rep. Laura Gillen (D-N.Y.) reposted Stansbury’s post, saying she was stuck behind the same police escort.

Rep. Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.) also said on X that he was stopped by a traffic incident, and has since entered a “no” vote into the record, indicating he opposed referring the impeachment to the judiciary committee and shutting it down.

“While en route to the floor to oppose that motion, a traffic incident and a police-escorted bus caused a delay that resulted in the vote closing before I, along with other Members, could reach the chamber,” Jackson wrote on X .

Rep. Marilyn Strickland (D-Wash.) did not release a public statement, but her chief of staff told a Politico reporter that she “was stuck behind a motorcade and missed the vote” by one minute, but would have voted no.

Rep. Brittany Pettersen (D-Colo.) did not release a public statement, but a spokesperson told Nexstar’s Denver station Fox 31 in a statement shared with The Hill that Pettersen “encountered a traffic incident,” blaming Republican leadership for closing the vote with absent members.

“While normally a floor vote is held open as a courtesy for the members who are near the Capitol and on their way to cast their votes, Republican leadership cynically chose to close the vote with nearly two dozen members still not voting — and just as Pettersen was reaching the chamber,” the spokesperson said.

Some Democrats who did vote slammed their colleagues for not showing up.

“There’s no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues,” Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.) told MeidasTouch. “This is what the people have been talking about … so shame on folks who were not here because these people lost.”

“I don’t know if anyone had any real health issues or anything significant to that respect, so I want to leave room for that, but that being said, at the end of the day we’re here to do a job,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez (D-N.Y.) said on CNN after the vote.

Other Democrats who missed the vote included Rep. Julia Brownley (D-Calif.), who said she was unable to vote but did not provide specifics. Rep. Lou Correa (D-Calif.) cited a medical issue while Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.) cited a personal emergency . Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) said she was in San Francisco for a Veterans Day event.

Reps. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) and Frederica Wilson (D-Fla.) did not release a statement on their absence and did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

While the effort to impeach Hegseth failed for now, Democrats will take a sizable majority in Congress starting in the new year, and could take up the effort again.

articles.title: Rand Paul plans to be top Republican on Senate health committee
articles.summary: Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) said Wednesday he is seeking the top GOP spot on the powerful Senate health committee next Congress, a move that would likely signal a major shift for the focus of Republicans on the panel. Paul, an ophthalmologist, is the most senior Republican on the panel. He is currently the chair of the…
articles.body:
Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) said Wednesday he is seeking the top GOP spot on the powerful Senate health committee next Congress, a move that would likely signal a major shift for the focus of Republicans on the panel.

Paul , an ophthalmologist, is the most senior Republican on the panel. He is currently the chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee but would give that up to move to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP).

The transition comes amid the fallout of a massive Republican electoral loss in the midterm elections that will reshape the committee. Current HELP Committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) lost his primary election earlier this year and other members, including Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), also lost.

“As a physician and the author of dozens of bills on health care, education, and labor, I know the issues before this committee affect nearly every American family, from the cost of health care and how schools serve our children to how people earn a living and save for retirement,” Paul said in a statement.

“[T]he coming Congress will bring a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen. Families, not federal bureaucrats, should make the decisions that shape their lives. I will stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks,” he added.

Paul is likely to spar with the incoming chair, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who has made expanding government-run healthcare — including moving towards Medicare for All — a major priority.

Paul would also be able to use his position in the minority to highlight medical positions many in the scientific community see as fringe, which he sees as evidence of bias.

As Homeland Security Committee chair, Paul said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”

Paul has relentlessly pursued investigations into the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic, blaming former COVID-19 czar Anthony Fauci for funding dangerous experiments in China and then covering up the evidence.

He tried to grill Fauci under oath in a hearing this summer, and then passed a resolution to indict Fauci for invoking his Fifth Amendment right to decline to answer questions, charging him with contempt of Congress.

articles.title: Haley rules out 2028 White House bid
articles.summary: Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley said she will not be making a presidential bid in 2028 but noted that she will continue to “push good policy” and “support good candidates.” “I am not running in 2028, but I will continue to talk about the things that I care about,” Haley said in an interview…
articles.body:
Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley said she will not be making a presidential bid in 2028 but noted that she will continue to “push good policy” and “support good candidates.”

“I am not running in 2028, but I will continue to talk about the things that I care about,” Haley said in an interview with CNBC . “I will continue to push good policy. I will continue to support good candidates, and we want a strong America.”

Haley’s remarks come as speculations continue to arise on the Republican presidential nominee for 2028. Some floating prominent names are Vice President Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, though no one has formally declared a bid.

Vance said last month that he would have President Trump’s endorsement he does run for the GOP presidential nomination in 2028, saying, “I think I would get his endorsement, but I also think there’s something to be said for people actually running their own race.”

The president did not explicitly say that he would endorse Vance but called him “a very talented person” and “very good person.”

Earlier last month, in an interview with NBC News, Vance said that it is “really obvious” that Cruz is going to be launching a presidential bid for 2028. Cruz previously sought presidential nomination in 2016 and was unsuccessful in his attempt.

“I’ll certainly be part of the discussion,” Cruz told MS NOW in August regarding the 2028 bid.

Rubio’s name has been floated as a possible GOP candidate for 2028, although earlier in September, he said that he has “no plans” to launch a presidential bid.

A day after the midterm elections, reports surfaced from outlets such as Bloomberg and the Independent , that said Rubio was weighing on leaving the Trump administration as he allegedly prepares a 2028 presidential run. The State Department dismissed the reports, calling them a “baseless hoax.”

Last week, the Democrats secured a stunning victory in the midterms, flipping GOP-held seats in battleground states like Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Maine and Iowa. The party will hold a majority in both chambers of Congress in January.

Haley, in her CNBC interview, called the midterm results “a total power move by the American people.”

“Republicans had the House, the Senate and the presidency for two years and they saw no change … I think they wanted to make everybody aware and they certainly did that,” she said noting high inflation, cost of living and interest rates.

“Now, the focus is what do you do with that?” Haley said. “Republicans need to hear the signs.”

articles.title: Sanders: ‘I will support’ Van Hollen for majority leader if he runs
articles.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said he would support Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) for majority leader if he chose to run following the independent saying he would not back Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the leadership role. “Look, I have known Chuck Schumer for a very long time. Actually, Chuck and I grew…
articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said he would support Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) for majority leader if he chose to run following the independent saying he would not back Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the leadership role.

“Look, I have known Chuck Schumer for a very long time. Actually, Chuck and I grew up in the same neighborhood, went to the same elementary school,” Sanders told “ The Weekly Show ” host Jon Stewart. “Do I think we need new leadership, which is going to move the Democratic Party in a much more vigorous way to protect the needs of working families? Yes, I do. Absolutely.”

The senator said he believed the American people “are sick and tired of the status quo.”

“We cannot have leadership in the Democratic Party who are going to do the same old, same old,” Sanders added.

“Chris Van Hollen is one guy who has indicated he might be interested in running for leader. If he chooses to do that, I will support him,” he concluded.

Van Hollen has flip-flopped on whether he will make a Senate leadership bid, though he said earlier this week he was “in listening mode” and has not “shut the door” on the possibility.

While Schumer has netted the backing of some veteran senators, many incoming and seasoned lawmakers remain divided on their support.

Sanders previously held a press conference alongside Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), where they both pledged to not support Schumer for Senate leadership. Sanders explained that he believed the current Senate minority leader had not been doing enough to end income and wealth inequality.

Democratic Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (Mich.), Troy Jackson (Maine) and Adam Hamilton (Kan.) similarly declined to back the New York Senator.

When asked about Schumer, Hamilton said many people in his home state found Schumer “ polarizing .”

“I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer,” the Kansas senator said. “And I’ve told him that as well. But I think, at least where I live in Kansas, he is kind of a polarizing figure.”

articles.title: House Democrat responds to White House warning: ‘Come at me, bro’
articles.summary: Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.) on Wednesday clapped back at the White House’s threat to investigate Democrats if they plan to probe President Trump and his administration, telling administration lawyers to “Come at me, bro.” “I just think we are so well situated to do our jobs. What they’re saying is: ‘Don’t do our jobs. Don’t…
articles.body:
Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.) on Wednesday clapped back at the White House’s threat to investigate Democrats if they plan to probe President Trump and his administration, telling administration lawyers to “Come at me, bro.”

“I just think we are so well situated to do our jobs. What they’re saying is: ‘Don’t do our jobs. Don’t do oversight. Don’t do check on the administration of the government,'” Lynch, a member of the House Oversight Committee, told CNN’s Pamela Brown.

The Boston native said that Congress passes laws and accused Trump of “habitually” violating those laws.

“So, we believe we have the right and we have been empowered expressly in the Constitution to make sure the president obeys the law,” Lynch continued. “This is pretty basic, and so that’s the core function … and I speak on behalf of the chairman in this respect, I’m sure.”

White House counsel Will Scharf wrote to incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on Monday that “abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas” are allegedly intended to “harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end.”

He asserted that any subpoenas could be criminal if they intend to deprive “citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges,” which could in of themselves could “warrant further investigation.”

Garcia claimed to reporters on Wednesday that Trump is “clearly hiding something” and said Oversight Democrats will not be intimidated.

“This idea that President Trump or the White House counsel want to send threatening letters to myself –– in which, of course, he threatens other members of Congress broadly –– is not only not constitutional, but it’s not going to stop the important work,” Garcia said.

The California Democrat added that voters chose accountability against alleged corruption that has kept prices high nationwide, as well as against other aspects of the president’s agenda like his deportation agenda.

Other lawmakers clapped back at Scharf’s warning. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who will serve as the chair of the House Judiciary Committee in the new Congress, told MeidasTouch that the “government cannot intimidate people because they exercise their First Amendment rights in a way that government officials don’t like, that is ridiculous.”

He said lawmakers will be exercising their constitutional duties “as the preeminent branch of government to conduct oversight operations of the entire government, as well as the economy and other things happening in society.”

“This is what they do, this is an act of desperation,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) also told MeidasTouch . “They are going after whoever they feel intimidated by, and we should not be afraid of them. We shouldn’t take the bait and we shouldn’t respond to them.”

Democrats have already launched several probes into alleged corruption in connection with Trump and his family, but Scharf said lawmakers need a legitimate legislative purpose underpinning any subpoena.

The latest back-and-forth comes after almost two years of Democrats accusing the Trump administration of improperly using levers of power, specifically via the Department of Justice, to investigate perceived foes of the president.

articles.title: Democrats investigate RFK Jr, donor over expensive gifts
articles.summary: Two Democratic senators launched a probe into Health and Human Services Secretary (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. this week after financial reports revealed he received over $250,000 in gifts last year from a former donor to his presidential campaign. In a letter addressed to the HHS secretary on Tuesday, Sens. Angela Alsobrooks (Md.) and Robert…
articles.body:
Two Democratic senators launched a probe into Health and Human Services Secretary (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. this week after financial reports revealed he received over $250,000 in gifts last year from a former donor to his presidential campaign.

In a letter addressed to the HHS secretary on Tuesday, Sens. Angela Alsobrooks (Md.) and Robert Wyden (Ore.) requested Kennedy provide more information about these gifts.

The Trump official reported the gifts from security consultant Gavin de Becker in his annual financial disclosure, including a $126,000 value for lodging at the donor’s Washington, D.C., home, $97,000 in flights to Fiji and $45,000 in flights to Greece.

The Wall Street Journal was the first to report on these gifts in September.

Alsobrooks and Wyden noted in their letter to the secretary that federal ethics rules prohibit federal officials from accepting gifts from a “ prohibited source .”

Prohibited sources are defined as people who “conducts activities regulated by the employee’s agency” or “has interests that may be substantially affected” by the employee’s official duties.

The lawmakers noted that de Becker has been a leading advocate for antivaccine causes and ketamine therapy.

“Mr. de Becker absolutely has vested interests in the outcome of decisions you make as Secretary,” they wrote. “As such, he is a prohibited source from whom you cannot lawfully accept gifts.”

Wyden is currently the ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee and is expected to take over the panel when Democrats gain power in the legislature next year.

De Becker, who provided security services to Kennedy and was a major contributor to his 2024 campaign, called the secretary his “closest friend in the world for many years” in a statement to The Wall Street Journal in September.

The senators also sent a separate letter to the security consultant on Tuesday, inquiring more details about his payments to Kennedy.

“Even if you consider Secretary Kennedy a friend, your relationship is not purely personal,” they wrote to de Becker, saying he had “vested interests in the outcome of decisions” made by the secretary.

The Hill has reached out to HHS for comment.

articles.title: Lankford says GOP will defer to Trump on next immigration push
articles.summary: Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.), who is poised to be a key player in any bipartisan immigration reform efforts in the next Congress, said he’s waiting for a signal from President Trump about what provisions to include. “The president has already said he wants to do something. I don’t know what that would be,” Lankford told…
articles.body:
Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.), who is poised to be a key player in any bipartisan immigration reform efforts in the next Congress, said he’s waiting for a signal from President Trump about what provisions to include.

“The president has already said he wants to do something. I don’t know what that would be,” Lankford told The Hill on Wednesday. “But right now, we’re all waiting to see what the president wants to do on that.”

Trump said in a CBS interview on Sunday that he’s interested in another go at bipartisan immigration reform with Democrats in charge.

Lankford is likely to be the top Republican on the Homeland Security committee, putting him squarely in the middle of any debate over immigration reform. Lankford is also close with Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, his former Senate delegation partner.

Lankford was a central broker of a 2024 bill with Sens. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) and then-Sen. Krysten Sinema (I-Ariz.) that included changes intended to process asylum claims faster and grant migrants work authorization more easily while strengthening security at the southern border, among other provisions.

That bill failed due to pressure from Trump ahead of the 2024 election, when his campaign made immigration a central issue. Lankford continued to defend the bill at the time, drawing further ire and threats of a 2028 primary challenge from Trump.

With Democrats in control, Lankford would likely need to work together with Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) if she is the new committee chair. Hassan hails from a purple state and has a history of bipartisan immigration work, including a bill focused on northern border security.

She was also one of a handful of Democrats who voted for a 2025 bill that mandates federal detainment of immigrants without legal status accused of theft and burglary among other crimes.

There’s reason to expect Democrats in the new majority could seek out a bipartisan deal that makes legal migration easier while cracking down on border security.

Several incoming Democratic freshmen from traditionally Republican states ran on a platform of securing the border while opposing the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement tactics.

articles.title: Massie secures signatures to force vote on second Epstein files petition
articles.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) announced he received enough signatures from lawmakers to force a vote on his discharge petition related to files of disgraced financier and convicted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein. “This morning we reached the required 218 signatures on my discharge petition for Epstein Files Transparency Act II,” Massie wrote on social media. Democrats Adam…
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) announced he received enough signatures from lawmakers to force a vote on his discharge petition related to files of disgraced financier and convicted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein.

“This morning we reached the required 218 signatures on my discharge petition for Epstein Files Transparency Act II,” Massie wrote on social media .

Democrats Adam Smith (Wash.) and John Garamendi (Calif.) were the final signatories, bringing it to 218.

The lawmaker said he was working closely with Reps. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) to “get this to the floor for a vote soon.”

Khanna — the original co-sponsor of the first Epstein files legislation — said earlier in September the new “Epstein 2.0 Act” would “allow state attorney generals to prosecute the pedophiles who abused and trafficked young girls.”

Massie similarly stated last week that this new act was intended to help survivors get “their own records” and enable state attorneys general to prosecute crimes related to the Epstein files. He added that the new legislation would also allow the Justice Department (DOJ) to be taken “to court for keeping critical files hidden.”

The initial Epstein Files Transparency Act forced the DOJ to release millions of files related to Epstein that implicated notable public figures.

But survivors and other backers called for greater transparency and additional prosecutions for Epstein’s co-conspirators.

Survivors also warned of the need for further redactions in the remaining files as the initial files, released by former Attorney General Pam Bondi, revealed the identities of some previously unknown victims. Released files also contained redactions of potential co-conspirators, which drew the ire of House Democrats.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the ranking member on the Oversight Committee, slammed the Justice Department on Tuesday for continuing “to illegally withhold over 2.5 million pages of documents.”

Garcia has pledged to hold public hearings for “uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump.”

He added that “our work is just getting started.”

The issue previously divided the GOP and created a rift between Massie’s bloc and President Trump, who protested its release for months.

Massie is racing the clock since he lost reelection in the lower chamber in the GOP primaries earlier this year to Trump-backed Rep.-elect Ed Gallerein (R-Ky.). He has aimed to complete much of his agenda in the House’s lame-duck session — including a failed bid to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

images.caption: Reps. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) speak to reporters outside a Department of Justice facility in Washington, D.C. on Feb. 9, 2026.

articles.title: Kiley calls for ‘reasonable’ bipartisan response to redistricting ‘plague’
articles.summary: Outgoing Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-Calif.), who left the Republican Party earlier this year over concerns of gerrymandering, is calling on lawmakers to find a solution to partisan redistricting — referring to the tactic as a “plague.” “I doubt the two sides will end this plague on our democracy anytime soon. But reasonable people of both…
articles.body:
Outgoing Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-Calif.), who left the Republican Party earlier this year over concerns of gerrymandering, is calling on lawmakers to find a solution to partisan redistricting — referring to the tactic as a “plague.”

“I doubt the two sides will end this plague on our democracy anytime soon. But reasonable people of both parties should at least be working on a solution for after the next Census,” Kiley wrote in a Wednesday post to social platform X .

Kiley lost the race for California’s 6th Congressional District to Democrat Richard Pan, a physician and former state senator. The state most recently redrew its congressional maps in November 2025, leaning five more House seats in Democrats’ favor.

The change actually diminished Democrats’ edge in California’s 6th District, becoming less blue in the new map, a Ballotpedia analysis found. But Kiley is projected to lose to his Democratic challenger, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), trailing behind Pan by over 18 percentage points with 81 percent of votes counted.

Kiley has been one of the most vocal critics of gerrymandering as both parties moved to redraw congressional districts ahead of the midterms. Ahead of Election Day, Republicans in Texas approved a new map aimed at helping GOP candidates, prompting California to temporarily adopt new congressional boundaries designed to help Democrats.

Republicans’ redistricting efforts broadly backfired , contributing to major losses in November’s midterms as Democrats swept up both chambers of the Congress — flipping GOP-held seats in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Maine and Iowa, among others.

Not only did the Democratic incumbents hold onto their seats, but in some states, the new maps went on to dilute the conservative vote in traditionally red districts. The trends were most visible in states like Texas, Ohio and North Carolina.

“It’s clear the Texas redistricting scheme accomplished nothing more than giving Gavin Newsom an excuse to re-gerrymander California (and perhaps contributed to Gov. Abbott’s defeat),” Kiley wrote in his Wednesday post.

He also lauded states like Indiana and South Carolina, crediting legislators “who refused to join the redistricting war actually saved their party seats.”

Republicans in both states rejected efforts to implement GOP-friendly maps. A DDHQ analysis showed that, if these maps had passed, they would have backfired — likely giving Democrats larger margins of victory.

articles.title: Delaware residents file lawsuit seeking second House seat
articles.summary: Two Delaware residents launched an attempt to add an additional House seat for the Diamond State in a Wednesday lawsuit against Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The 21-page complaint was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia by University of Delaware professor David Redlawsk and resident Kevin Price. Plaintiffs argue that the…
articles.body:
Two Delaware residents launched an attempt to add an additional House seat for the Diamond State in a Wednesday lawsuit against Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

The 21-page complaint was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia by University of Delaware professor David Redlawsk and resident Kevin Price.

Plaintiffs argue that the state’s one at-large House seat, currently occupied by Rep. Sarah McBride (D-Del.), is not enough for the state’s roughly 991,000 residents.

The complaint names Lutnick because the Commerce Department oversees the Census, which is used to determine the number of House seats based on state population count. Commerce Deputy Undersecretary George Cook and House Clerk Kevin McCumber are also named in the lawsuit.

Attorneys for Redlawsk and Price requested that a three-judge panel at the federal court declare the 435-seat limitation imposed under the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929 unconstitutional in order to permit the body to grow to a total of 436 seats.

“The 435-seat limitation imposes a severe and avoidable disparity on Delaware’s voters,” the lawsuit says. “A second Delaware seat would satisfy the Constitution’s requirements for whole seats, State boundaries, and at least one Representative for every State.”

The Hill has reached out to the Commerce Department for comment.

Delaware is one of five U.S. states with only one representative in the House, including Alaska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming.

The lawsuit notes that “no state holds a smaller share of the House relative to its share of the Nation’s population.” The plaintiffs’ attorneys point to the fact that Montana, which has less than 100,000 more residents than Delaware, has two seats in the lower chamber of Congress.

“Delaware’s allocation results from Congress’s retention of a House size fixed in 1911, when the Nation had less than one-third its present population,” the lawsuit says. “That retention lacks a sufficient justification.”
