articles.title: The Memo: Misfire on Hegseth vote adds to Democratic tensions
articles.summary: Democrats admit they fumbled Tuesday when they allowed House Republicans to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Now the question is whether the embarrassing misfire can be chalked up to one-off disorganization or is symptomatic of a larger problem. Among progressives, irritation goes beyond the specifics of the failure of the Hegseth…
articles.body:
Democrats admit they fumbled Tuesday when they allowed House Republicans to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Now the question is whether the embarrassing misfire can be chalked up to one-off disorganization or is symptomatic of a larger problem.

Among progressives, irritation goes beyond the specifics of the failure of the Hegseth effort and into a broader critique of the leadership of their own party, which they often contend is ineffective.

Corbin Trent, a progressive strategist and the executive director of a leftist super PAC A Fight Worth Having, is among those who condemn the Hegseth failure as emblematic of a deeper weakness.

Trent pointed the finger at House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is widely expected to become Speaker in the new Congress.

“It’s yet another signal that Leader Jeffries isn’t up to the task,” Trent told this column.

Jeffries, in the immediate aftermath of the vote, had told reporters, “This is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning.”

Trent, who several years ago served as communications director for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), added that the result of last week’s midterm elections should not give Democrats any grounds of complacency.

The election, he contended, was “a repudiation of the way things are done, and it appears that message was not received. Too many Democrats think they were chosen. I think Republicans were rejected far more than Democrats were chosen.”

The core of the Hegseth issue is a Tuesday vote in which Republicans were attempting to bottle up an effort to impeach Hegseth. The impeachment push came from one of their own members — Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), a libertarian who has been a strong critic of President Trump, particularly over the war on Iran.

There was never any chance that a significant number of Republicans would back Massie. But prior to the vote, speculation had centered upon whether Republican absences would allow the maverick Kentuckian’s measure to advance.

To the surprise of almost everyone, more Democrats than Republicans missed the vote, with 11 Democrats failing to show. That allowed the GOP to kill the impeachment effort — at least for now.

There is a theoretical possibility Massie could try again, and a more plausible scenario in which Democrats impeach Hegseth once they assume the majority in the new Congress.

Still, Tuesday’s debacle sparked a chaotic 24 hours, in which several of the nonvoting Democrats have said that they were stuck in traffic. Some have suggested the House vote should have been kept open longer than it was.

The office of Democratic Rep. Melanie Stansbury (N.M.) said that “like other Members of Congress,” the congresswoman was “blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due to a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote.”

Another Democrat who missed the vote, Rep. Jonathan Jackson (Ill.), wrote on social media Tuesday that those same factors “caused a delay that resulted in the vote closing before I, along with other Members, could reach the chamber.”

Jackson reiterated, “I remain firm in my position that Secretary Hegseth must be held accountable and impeached.”

But the irritation about the missed votes was plain to hear, especially from more progressive members.

Ocasio-Cortez told CNN’s Manu Raju that she wanted to “leave room” for the possibility that some members who failed to vote had health issues or other significant challenges. But, she added, “At the end of the day, we’re here to do a job. And the same way I had to clock in when I worked at a restaurant, we got to clock in and do our work here.”

Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.) was even more forceful, telling MeidasTouch’s Pablo Manríquez , “We knew this vote was coming, so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote.”

In an interview Tuesday night with CNN’s Laura Coates , Democratic Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (N.C.) said of the nonvoting members, “I say shame on them for not showing up … They had an opportunity to finally get rid of this buffoonery that we have, you know, and they failed.”

Ojeda said he would vote to impeach if the measure came up once the new Congress is sworn in. In that scenario, Democrats may reframe, or simply reuse, the charges that Massie was seeking to bring against Hegseth.

Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment , three of which related to Hegseth allegedly leading the war on Iran without the requisite congressional approval. Other articles encompassed topics like the boat strikes in the Caribbean that have killed more than 200 people; the reported killings of more than 100 schoolchildren in an airstrike on a school in Minab, Iran; and the seizure of Nicolás Maduro, then the president of Venezuela, in January.

Hegseth has fought back hard against the effort, characterizing it as motivated by personal grievance on Massie’s behalf, and as part of a broader anti-Trump effort. The president has forcefully backed his Defense secretary.

But whatever is to come in January, annoyance among liberal and left-leaning figures about Tuesday’s failed vote can’t be ignored.

“This is something Democrats campaigned hard on, they’ve made clear they intend to impeach Pete Hegseth,” said Matthew Duss, the executive vice president at the Center for International Policy and a former adviser to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) “Just a few days after a massive wave election, to see something like this was kind of dispiriting.”

Duss added that he saw the episode as a “failure of leadership.”

Democratic strategist Basil Smikle said: “Maybe this one is the mulligan, but once the new Congress starts there is going to be a lot more accountability going on. It’s going to be really important for Hakeem Jeffries to keep his conference focused and aligned.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Ohio Republicans loosen regulations on gun silencers, sawed-off shotguns
articles.summary: Ohio Republicans passed legislation Tuesday easing restrictions on silencers and short-barreled firearms, moving to roll back certain state gun laws just days after Democrats swept last week’s midterm elections. The measure, which includes loosening rules on “sawed-off shotguns,” passed both chambers of the Republican-controlled legislature largely along party lines and is now awaiting the signature…
articles.body:
Ohio Republicans passed legislation Tuesday easing restrictions on silencers and short-barreled firearms, moving to roll back certain state gun laws just days after Democrats swept last week’s midterm elections.

The measure, which includes loosening rules on “sawed-off shotguns,” passed both chambers of the Republican-controlled legislature largely along party lines and is now awaiting the signature of outgoing Gov. Mike DeWine (R).

The vote marks lawmakers’ first major legislative action since the GOP suffered widespread election losses last week. It also comes ahead of a new legislative session in January, when a Democrat — Gov.-elect Amy Acton — will take the governor’s mansion, and her party will also have a greater presence in the Ohio Statehouse.

Under current Ohio law, silencers, short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns are classified as “dangerous ordnance.” Possessing them is generally prohibited unless gun owners comply with federal registration requirements, which include an additional background check and a $200 tax.

The measure would remove the registration requirement from state law, aligning with recent federal changes that have thrown longstanding restrictions on the weapons into question .

Republicans argued the existing rules impose unnecessary burdens on lawful gun owners without making Ohioans safer.

“This is in no way shape or form anything that’s going to make Ohio less safe,” state Rep. Tex Fischer (R) said Tuesday.

Democrats who opposed the legislation questioned why lawmakers were prioritizing expanding gun rights over addressing gun violence and the rising living costs.

“I have a young man, literally just get shot steps from my house. And we are here today talking about this bill,” said state Rep. Darnell Brewer (D) , ahead of a committee vote. “We need to save lives in Ohio.”

The legislation comes amid a broader legal fight over the National Firearms Act, the nearly century-old federal law regulating silencers and short-barreled firearms.

Congress eliminated the $200 federal tax on these weapons through President Trump’s sweeping tax and spending law last year, prompting a legal challenge to the remaining registration requirements.

articles.title: Democrats, vowing action next year, stew over missed votes on Hegseth impeachment
articles.summary: House Democrats are steaming after 11 colleagues missed a vote to impeach Pete Hegseth, allowing the Defense secretary’s Republican allies to defeat the measure this week. The debacle is leading to new calls for Democrats to tighten the ship when it comes to demanding attendance for floor votes. And it’s providing new fuel to a…
articles.body:
House Democrats are steaming after 11 colleagues missed a vote to impeach Pete Hegseth, allowing the Defense secretary’s Republican allies to defeat the measure this week.

The debacle is leading to new calls for Democrats to tighten the ship when it comes to demanding attendance for floor votes. And it’s providing new fuel to a growing chorus of Democrats who want to prioritize Hegseth’s impeachment early next year when they’ll control both chambers of Congress — a push that could pose a headache for party leaders who are proposing a more deliberate approach to executive oversight.

“It’s absolutely unacceptable that any vote would be lost on absences, like just period. It’s totally unacceptable, and we need to raise it up back again as soon as possible and make sure everyone gets on it,” progressive firebrand Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) said.

“We got to do our job. We got to show up. We got to get these things done, and that’s just the fact of the matter. We got to do the job. We got to clock in. This is what we’re here to do,” she added.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) delivered a similar message.

“On important votes, we’ve got to make clear that people have to come,” he said.

Khanna is among the growing list of lawmakers who want to vote quickly on Hegseth’s impeachment again next year when Democrats control the House floor.

“We should do it as soon as we can,” he said.

Asked if Democrats need hearings or investigations before bringing the measure to the floor, Khanna didn’t miss a beat.

That strategy sets the stage for a clash with Democratic leaders, who say they’re opposed to “snap” impeachments. While they supported the Hegseth resolution this week, they didn’t bring it to the floor themselves. And in the majority next year, they say they want to conduct deep-dive examinations of various Trump officials before jumping to impeachment.

Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), who is in line to become the next House majority leader, said Democratic leaders have no plans to revisit Hegseth’s impeachment next year.

“When we are in the majority, we are serious about holding people accountable, and that will … start early with oversight,” Aguilar said. “But that is not anything that is being discussed at this point.”

The uproar came after Republicans blocked eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, which were sponsored by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.), when they came to the floor on Tuesday evening. The vote was 211-204, but 11 Democrats missed the vote. If eight of those lawmakers had been on the floor, the impeachment effort would have advanced.

Some of the 11 Democrats, including Reps. Melanie Stansbury (N.M.) and Jonathan Jackson (Ill.), said they were stuck in a traffic jam and couldn’t reach the House chamber on time.

Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s (D-Calif.) office said in a statement that she had been at a Veterans Day event in San Francisco but supports impeaching Hegseth and would have voted no on the motion to refer.

Nevada Rep. Steven Horsford (D) said in remarks Wednesday that a “personal emergency” delayed his arrival on the House floor and that he takes “full responsibility.”

Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) said she was furious at the no-shows, warning that voters who just handed Democrats their majority will expect more in the next Congress.

“I understand there was difficulty getting to the Capitol because of an accident. But we’ve got to stay on our game, especially being in the majority, [to] make sure that we deliver the votes,” she said.

Tlaib is also pushing to impeach Hegseth early next year.

“Absolutely — we have to,” she said. “I think it sets a dangerous precedent when we allow someone to move in a way that is against the best interests of the country.”

“I think everybody needs to be here for all votes, right? I mean, that’s an important vote. I don’t know what would have made the difference. I don’t think it would have made the difference. That doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t all be here to vote for it,” Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) said.

All the Democrats who voted Tuesday decided against sending Massie’s resolution to committee.

“I think you saw yesterday how Democrats feel about the danger that Pete Hegseth poses to the American people, the worst Defense secretary, in my view, in the history of the United States, and I don’t think he’s fit to serve,” Rep. Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.) said, noting that he’s sure the conference will have a discussion “in the next several weeks” on how to move forward.

Massie introduced the articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, arguing that he abused his authority by waging a war in Iran without congressional authorization, seizing the Venezuelan president from his own country and overseeing the extrajudicial killings of alleged drug smugglers in international waters.

Massie had launched an effort to impeach Hegseth back in September, but House GOP leaders canceled votes and sent lawmakers home early, which allowed them to avoid a vote on Massie’s resolution.

He told Politico he doesn’t plan on reintroducing articles of impeachment against Hegseth on the floor again.

Hegseth defended himself during a presser Tuesday, arguing that Massie’s effort was a “political spectacle” and a “personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”

“In the 250 years of our American republic, no secretary of war or secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations,” Hegseth said. “And in our case, successful ones at that. Not once. War powers resolution or not. The history is clear and it’s very straightforward. And one disgruntled congressman wants to shred it over policy disagreements.”

“That’s what it is. Policy disagreements.”

articles.title: Colom builds on slim lead in Mississippi, as AP calls for Democrat
articles.summary: Democrat Scott Colom has built on his lead in the closely watched Mississippi Senate race, now ahead of Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) by nearly 4,500 votes, or about half a percentage point. The latest batch of votes came as heavily Democratic Hinds County wraps up counting its absentee and affidavit ballots. The county, which includes…
articles.body:
Democrat Scott Colom has built on his lead in the closely watched Mississippi Senate race, now ahead of Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) by nearly 4,500 votes, or about half a percentage point.

The latest batch of votes came as heavily Democratic Hinds County wraps up counting its absentee and affidavit ballots. The county, which includes the capital of Jackson, rejected most of its affidavit ballots Wednesday.

Still, the added votes pushed Colom even further ahead, though the race remains close.

CNN and The Associated Press projected Colom as the winner Wednesday afternoon, but Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s election desk partner, has not yet projected a winner.

Colom maintained throughout the counting process that he believed he was on track to win, telling CNN Monday that he is “ready to serve.” Hyde-Smith told CBS News she felt “very optimistic.”

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), released a statement congratulating Colom Wednesday after other outlets called him the winner.

“Congratulations to Senator-Elect Colom on his historic win and on becoming the first Democrat to win a Mississippi Senate seat in over four decades,” Gillibrand said. “We will work hand in hand with Scott to fight for Mississippians’ health care, costs, and future in the 120th Congress and look forward to welcoming him to our caucus.”

There are still ballots left to count in the state, but all ballots that were mailed by Election Day had to arrive by Monday in order to be counted. Mississippi’s secretary of state said Wednesday that 23 of the state’s 82 counties have uploaded their certified results, and that the deadline for all counties to do so is Friday.

The secretary also said that nearly 19,000 affidavit ballots have already been processed, though it is not clear how many remain.

If the Mississippi Democrat does go on to win, it would be a seismic shift in the traditionally Republican Deep South.

Mississippi has never elected a Black senator by popular vote, but had two Black Republicans elected by the legislature during reconstruction. The state was central to the fight for civil and voting rights throughout the 1960s.

A pickup for Democrats in the Magnolia State would not only be an upset, but it would push their gains in the Senate to an eight-seat pickup, with the potential to make Alaska — also still outstanding — a ninth.

Colom and Hyde-Smith have history going back at least a few years. President Biden nominated Colom to serve as a federal judge, but Hyde-Smith used her ability as his home-state senator to block him from receiving a confirmation hearing.

Now, Colom has the chance to block her from seeking a second full term.

articles.body:
GOP presses ahead with Heidi Overton nomination

When we last saw Heidi Overton in the Senate HELP Committee, she was dodging difficult questions from senators during her confirmation hearing in September.

It’s not clear if she has the votes to advance to the floor, but Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) scheduled a vote on her nomination for next Wednesday, along with James O’Neill’s nomination to serve as director of the National Science Foundation.

Cassidy says he still isn’t sure how he’ll vote. One way or the other, the process is advancing.

“While I remain undecided on both of their nominations and am aware that other Republican members of the Committee are undecided as well, the Committee is moving forward with noticing their markup in the hopes of resolving their path forward one way or another this Congress,” Cassidy wrote on the social platform X

Republicans have just a single vote majority on the panel, so losing one member would be enough to sink the nomination if all Democrats oppose it.

“Over the last several months, I have had several frank conversations with both Dr. Overton and Mr. O’Neill about their visions, roles, and the lack of trust that exists due to broken promises and irresponsible decisions from other officials within the Administration,” Cassidy said. “I appreciate their ongoing candid conversations.”

The September hearing shed light on the priorities of lawmakers but offered little about Overton’s views and how she would run the sprawling agency responsible for drug, tobacco and vaccine regulation, as well as the safety of much of the food supply.

Cassidy previously criticized Overton’s involvement in the Trump administration’s efforts to roll back childhood vaccination , calling it “almost disqualifying.” He indicated Overton would need to repudiate Trump’s comments to secure his vote.

The Louisiana senator has repeatedly tried to extract promises from administration health nominees to uphold scientific standards and not upend vaccine policy, to little avail.

articles.title: Mississippi Senate stunner: Cindy Hyde-Smith concedes to Democrat Scott Colom
articles.summary: Democrat Scott Colom is set to become Mississippi’s next senator after Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith conceded Wednesday, notching a major victory for his party in the ruby red state. “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said in a video posted to…
articles.body:
Democrat Scott Colom is set to become Mississippi’s next senator after Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith conceded Wednesday, notching a major victory for his party in the ruby red state.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said in a video posted to social media Wednesday evening. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

Hyde-Smith, who was endorsed by President Trump, was seeking a second term as the Magnolia State’s junior senator. A Democrat has not won a Senate seat in the state since 1982, and the incumbent was favored to win the race.

The race was too close to call the week after Election Day as the Democrat held a razor-thin lead over the incumbent. The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projected the race for Colom shortly after Hyde-Smith conceded Wednesday. He notched 49.18 percent of the vote while the incumbent garnered about 48. 72 percent, with 95 percent of the vote tallied by DDHQ.

Colom’s victory further cushions Democrats’ newfound majority in the Senate after flipping key red seats in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and Iowa. The battleground Alaska Senate seat is still up for grabs, though Democrat Mary Peltola has pulled ahead of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in recent days.

Democrats in Mississippi expressed confidence as the final votes were tallied, though the race could be headed for the courts.

“I am very happy with where we stand. I’m confident once the process plays out, where we are, where the ballots are, we’re going to win,” Colom told reporters the Wednesday after Election Day.

There is no automatic recount procedure in the state, and Hyde-Smith’s narrow loss is likely to spark legal action from the Republican.

Lawyers for the Senate GOP’s campaign arm have already demanded that the state’s election officials preserve records and provisional ballots. Lawyers for Colom, a district attorney, called the move “unlawful.”

The Democrat notched notable support from national Democrats in his quest to flip the seat, including an endorsement from former President Obama. Former Vice President Harris also stumped for him ahead of the election.

Trump visited the state in the days ahead of the election to boost Hyde-Smith.

Colom’s victory points to frustration among Republican voters in the red stronghold amid rising costs and the president’s souring approval ratings. Colom also homed in on Black voters in the state that boasts the highest population in the country.

“We’ve been gifted an opportunity,” Colom told The Associated Press in October, pointing to the political climate and the strong base of Black voters in the state.

He is the first Black senator from the state since the Reconstruction Era.

The senator-elect has a tense history with Hyde-Smith. In 2023, the Mississippi Republican blocked his lifetime appointment to a federal district court, The New York Times reported in May. He told the outlet that he likely wouldn’t have run for Congress if he had been confirmed to the court.

Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018 after then-Sen. Thad Cochran (R) resigned. She won a full term in 2020 by about 10 percentage points.

Cook Political Report and DDHQ forecasted the seat would almost surely remain in Republican hands in the lead-up to the election.

articles.title: Interior plans public land sales
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Interior eyes public land sales and workforce change The Trump administration is planning to sell some public lands in the years ahead, it announced this week. © AP Photo/Alex Brandon The Interior Department “will work to decrease the size of the federal estate by…
articles.body:
Interior eyes public land sales and workforce change

The Trump administration is planning to sell some public lands in the years ahead, it announced this week.

The Interior Department “will work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands,” said a new strategic department plan for the years 2026 through 2030.

“Through these sales, the Department will be able to focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands,” it said.

The report added that “a portion” of the money from these sales could go back to the purchaser “for conservation purposes elsewhere in the state, locality or Tribal land, leading to improved recreation access for American citizens, while at the same time decreasing the federal taxpayer’s financial responsibility to manage federal lands.”

In addition, the plan says the department will “consolidate its workforce.” It did not say what exactly this would entail, and spokespeople for the department did not respond to a question from The Hill about whether this would mean layoffs.

The department also did not respond to questions about the land sales.

However, Kate Groetzinger, communications director at the Center for Western Priorities, expressed concern that while the plan calls for selling lands to states and localities, lands could be resold to private companies.

“There’s nothing stopping a state or a local government or a tribe from turning around and selling land to a private developer,” Groetzinger said.

“Public lands are part of the culture and the lifestyle out west, and a lot of the lands that developers might be interested in would be land that’s near communities, and that’s the lands that people use to recreate on most often,” she added.

Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, has yet to call the race, but as of Wednesday evening, Smith led Murphy by less than…
articles.body:
Rep. Greg Murphy (R-N.C.) conceded his reelection race on Wednesday to Democrat Raymond Smith, flipping another House seat for Democrats after a close contest in North Carolina’s 3rd Congressional District.

Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, has yet to call the race , but as of Wednesday evening, Smith led Murphy by less than 300 votes after trailing the GOP lawmaker by even fewer votes on election night. Provisional ballots helped ease Murphy’s narrow lead and put Smith ahead.

“I want to congratulate Representative-Elect Raymond Smith on his successful election for the Third District Congressional seat,” Murphy said in a statement . “I am sure he will serve the next two years with honor and integrity.”

Murphy, who has represented the eastern North Carolina district since 2019, thanked his supporters and said serving in Congress had been the greatest honor of his life.

“I would be remiss if I did not express personal disappointment in not being able to continue what I believe was good and diligent work on behalf of the people of eastern North Carolina,” his statement reads.

Smith, an army veteran and former state lawmaker, celebrated the win on Wednesday, thanking volunteers and voters who supported his campaign.

“This victory doesn’t belong to me. It belongs to the people who believed in something greater than themselves,” Smith said in a post on the social platform X .

“Whether you may have voted for me or not, I intend to work just as hard for you,” he added. “Our communities deserve to be heard in Washington, and I’m ready to get to work.”

Murphy had already declared victory a day after the election, despite thousands of ballots still awaiting counting. In a social media post at the time, he said he was “honored to be reelected by the good people of the Third District,” describing the race as a razor-thin victory.

Smith disputed the declaration at the time, pointing to roughly 6,000 provisional ballots that had yet to be counted across the district’s nine counties. His campaign also began seeking donations to prepare for a possible recount.

articles.body:
Rep.-elect Zach Dembo (D-Ky.) said it would be “premature” to discuss Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s impeachment following a failed House vote to oust the head of the Pentagon.

“Look, I just got elected a week ago. I don’t even have an office yet. I’ll tell you, I did not come here with the goal of impeachment. I came here with the goal of driving down costs and fighting corruption,” Dembo told MS NOW’s Peter Alexander.

“I’ll tell you, I’m worried about a lot of things that came out of the Pentagon,” the incoming lawmaker continued. “And so I’m certainly interested in making sure there’s accountability in the 120th, but it’s premature at this point without having seen what the articles are.”

Dembo cited his past experience as a former Navy Judge Advocate and federal prosecutor in the Justice Department as reasoning as to why he is “never going to speculate without seeing the evidence first.”

“But let me tell you, I think accountability at the Pentagon has to be a priority of the 120th,” he concluded.

His remarks come after House Republicans were able to shelve Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) eight impeachment articles against Hegseth.

The articles focused on Hegseth’s leadership during the ongoing war with Iran and accused him of abusing his powers in relation to several other Pentagon operations, including the seizure of the Venezuelan president from his own country and the extrajudicial killings of alleged drug smugglers in international waters.

Republicans benefitted from 11 Democrats who missed the consequential vote. Of the group, some cited conflicting engagements and being stuck in traffic, which drew ire from their Democratic colleagues.

Massie was ousted from his seat by a Trump-backed candidate, though Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) — a frequent collaborator of the outgoing Republican lawmaker — has indicated Hegseth’s impeachment is a top priority in a press conference Tuesday.

Other Democrats have similarly listed the defense secretary’s ousting as critical as the party prepares to take control of the lower chamber. Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) told NewsNation Tuesday evening that she believed Hegseth’s days “ are numbered .”

Meanwhile, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) predicted Hegseth will either resign, be fired or be impeached in the second half of President Trump’s term.

articles.summary: Sen. The Missouri senator listed his five priorities for his party in a post to the social platform X, including passing…
articles.body:
Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) is calling on the Senate to pass a moratorium on data center construction in the period before Republicans lose the majority , the first GOP senator to call for the move nationwide.

The Missouri senator listed his five priorities for his party in a post to the social platform X, including passing a major voting bill that President Trump urged Republicans to pass for much of this year.

“Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks? Here you go: DEFUND Planned Parenthood, MORATORIUM on data centers, SUSPEND the gas tax, FUND rural hospitals, SAVE AMERICA ACT,” Hawley wrote.

Hawley, known for his more populist brand, may find more support from Democrats on some of those issues, like a data center moratorium or funding rural hospitals — something Democrats have slammed Republicans for due to the impact of Trump’s signature tax bill .

He may not find much assistance from Democrats on other issues, but data centers became a flashpoint in the midterms, and a campaign issue that seemed not to fall cleanly along party lines.

In Texas, GOP Gov. Greg Abbott broke with some in his party — including the president — and halted new data center construction pending a statewide audit after his Democratic opponent, now-Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, campaigned against him on the issue.

Democratic candidates in South Carolina and Ohio also hit their GOP opponents hard on data centers. Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.) nicknamed Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) “data center Darline” in a debate, and also called for a two-year moratorium.

And as Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) attacked Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) for his past support for data centers, Husted pushed the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill aimed at mitigating data center electricity costs. But Democrats ultimately blocked its passage in the Senate, denying Husted a political win before an election.

Data centers steadily became more unpopular with voters throughout this year.

A Pew Research poll from the summer found a majority of voters believe data centers are bad for the environment, and half said they were bad for home energy costs — both shares were significant increases from Pew’s January survey.

And the poll did not find significant differences of opinion across party lines. Sixty-eight percent of Democrats and 54 percent of Republicans said they were not comfortable with a new local data center.

articles.body:
What Tech Oversight Project wants to see from Democrats in the first 100 days

The Tech Oversight Project is offering a blueprint for Democrats in the new Congress after what it described as the “first AI and tech accountability election.”

In a memo shared first with The Hill, the tech watchdog group urged the party to keep up the pressure on major tech firms and bring forward legislation on social media, AI and data centers .

Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project, suggested in Wednesday’s memo that the “worst thing Democrats could do now is return to business as usual with Big Tech.”

She called on the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to quickly schedule oversight hearings with leading tech executives, name AI safety champions to committee leadership roles and pledge to refuse AI super PAC money.

Also on the agenda — comprehensive social media and AI safety legislation, new requirements for how data center developers handle energy costs and restrictions on bailouts for AI companies.

Despite the difficulties of legislating in the new Congress, the memo suggested such measures could garner bipartisan support or force Republicans to go on the record with votes.

Get the full breakdown of the project’s recs at TheHill.com .
